blocks.text: Diabetes mellitus is a clinical syndrome characterized by persistently high blood glucose values due to deficiency or diminished effectiveness of insulin.
Diabetes mellitus can be classified as follows:
Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) – due to autoimmune β-cell destruction
Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) – due to a progressive loss of β-cell insulin secretion frequently with underlying insulin resistance

blocks.text: Main clinical features of diabetes are thirst, polydipsia, polyuria, tiredness, loss of weight, blurring of vision.

Many people have no classical symptoms and may only present late with the symptoms related to complications e.g., pruritus vulvae and balanitis due to infections, paresthesia or pain in the limbs, non-healing ulcers, and recurrent bacterial infections.

Self-Monitoring Blood Glucose (SMBG) is usually recommended in the following patients:
Patients on insulin and glucose lowering agents that can cause hypoglycemia (sulphonylureas)
When monitoring hyperglycemia arising from illness
When changes in treatment, lifestyle or other conditions requires data on glycemic patterns
When HbA1c estimations are unreliable (e.g. haemoglobinopathies).

blocks.text: Correct perioperative management depends on type of surgery (major or minor), type of diabetes and recent diabetes control. A perioperative HBA1c, fasting or random blood glucose is recommended to assess glycemic control and identify undiagnosed diabetes
Surgery should be delayed if possible if HBA1C >9% or blood glucose fasting >10 mmol/l or random glucose > 13 mmol/l.
Screen for nephropathy, cardiac disease, retinopathy and neuropathy and inform surgical team.
Optimal glycemic target in the perioperative period should be to maintain blood glucose levels between 7.8-10mmol/l
If diabetes is well controlled and surgery is minor:
If on oral agent therapy, omit therapy on morning of surgery except SGLTS2 inhibitors which should be stopped 24 to 72hour before surgery and resume therapy when eating normally

blocks.text: For T1DM, continue with normal basal dose of insulin, the short acting or rapid acting insulins can be given as per correctional scale insulin.

Decrease the dose of long-acting basal insulin by 20% to 25% the evening before surgery. If they routinely take basal insulin only in the morning, the reduced dose should instead be administered on the morning of surgery.
